lead: The charging system keeps the 12 V bus alive while the engine runs. Belts spin an alternator, which makes three-phase AC; a rectifier turns it into DC. A voltage regulator adjusts field current so the bus stays near 14 V, high enough to charge the battery and run lights, ECUs and pumps. It matters because the battery alone cannot supply a long drive. Every petrol or diesel car uses this loop, and the same idea appears in agricultural pumpsets and small generators.
prereq: You need: battery voltage and capacity from Chapter 1.2 and Chapter 1.3, plus the idea that diodes turn AC into DC.

blocks.text: The charging system is a closed loop. The engine belt turns the alternator. The alternator produces three-phase AC. A diode rectifier converts that AC into DC. The DC bus feeds the battery and every load. The regulator watches bus voltage and adjusts alternator field current. More field current means more generated voltage and current; less field current means less.

The target is a bus voltage of about 13.8 V to 14.4 V at normal temperature. This is above a rested 12 V battery (about 12.4 V to 12.7 V), so current flows into the battery. A fully charged battery needs only a small current. After a start, the battery accepts a large current for a short time. The regulator does not fix current; it fixes voltage, and current follows Ohm's law and the battery's state.

Temperature matters. A cold battery accepts charge at a higher voltage without gassing much, so some regulators raise the set point in cold weather. A hot battery needs a lower set point to avoid water loss. The nominal 14.2 V figure is a common room-temperature value, not a universal constant. The rotor and stator details are in Chapter 1.5.

sections.h3: Terminals, lamp and first field current

items: B+ is battery positive: thick cable from rectifier output to battery positive and main fuse box.
B− is battery negative: return through engine block, chassis and battery negative.
D+ is field or excitation: feeds the rotor field winding.
L is lamp: joins the charge warning lamp to the ignition switch.
Sense is a thin voltage-sense wire, often marked S or internal to B+.

blocks.text: At key-on, engine off, the ignition switch sends battery voltage to the lamp. Current goes from battery positive, through the ignition switch, through the lamp, into L and D+, through the field winding, and out through the regulator to ground. This small current creates a weak magnetic field. It is called initial excitation. The lamp glows because current flows through it.

When the engine starts, the alternator begins to generate. D+ voltage rises. With about 14 V on both sides of the lamp, the lamp goes out. The alternator now supplies its own field current through the rectifier diodes. The warning lamp is therefore both a check lamp and an excitation path. If the bulb is open, the alternator may not start charging, even though the belt is tight.

Other parts complete the circuit. A fuse protects the B+ cable and the sense wire. The ignition switch controls the lamp circuit. Grounds at the engine block, chassis and battery negative must be clean; a high-resistance ground makes the regulator see a low voltage and overcharge. The voltage sense wire may go to the battery positive or to a main junction. It carries almost no current; it only tells the regulator the true bus voltage.

sections.h3: Current paths at low and high load

blocks.text: At low load, the battery is charged and few accessories are on. The regulator reduces field current. The alternator output is just enough to hold the bus at the set point and supply small loads. The battery current is near zero or a few amperes. The warning lamp stays off.

At high load, headlamps, wipers, blower and ECUs draw current. Bus voltage falls a little. The regulator increases field current. Alternator output rises. The battery may supply current for a short time if the alternator cannot keep up, especially at idle. Once engine speed rises, the alternator takes over and recharges the battery.

Current paths are simple. Supply path: alternator B+ → fusible link or fuse → battery positive → loads. Return path: load → chassis ground → engine block → B− → battery negative. The regulator senses bus voltage between B+ and ground. It changes field current in the rotor; it does not change engine speed. Raising engine speed only raises the alternator's available output, not the regulated voltage.

blocks.where: I<sub>charge</sub> is charging current in A; V<sub>reg</sub> is regulated bus voltage in V; V<sub>oc</sub> is battery open-circuit voltage in V; R<sub>internal</sub> is battery internal resistance in Ω.

figure.caption: The belt drives the alternator, and the rectifier turns its AC into DC for the bus. Notice the dashed sense line: the regulator reacts to bus voltage by changing field current.

spec.title: Charging circuit
spec.aria: A charging block diagram runs from engine belt to alternator, rectifier and DC bus, with the regulator sensing bus voltage and controlling alternator field current.

examples.question: A car alternator is regulated at 14.2 V. The battery open-circuit voltage is 12.4 V and its internal resistance is 0.02 Ω. Neglect wiring resistance. Find the initial charging current.
steps: Driving voltage for charge = V<sub>reg</sub> − V<sub>oc</sub> = 14.2 V − 12.4 V = 1.8 V.
Initial charging current I = 1.8 V ÷ 0.02 Ω = 90 A.
As the battery charges, V<sub>oc</sub> rises toward 14.2 V, so the current falls.
examples.answer: The initial charging current is 90 A, and it falls as the battery charges.
examples.check:
v_reg = 14.2
v_oc = 12.4
r_int = 0.02
i_charge = (v_reg - v_oc) / r_int
print(i_charge)

traps: The regulator controls field current, not engine speed. Revving the engine does not raise the regulated bus voltage above its set point.
A dead charge warning lamp can stop charging because it supplies initial field current on many machines.
Do not use open-circuit battery voltage as the charging voltage. A 12 V battery at rest is about 12.4 V; the bus runs near 14 V.
The B− path is not just the thin wire. Engine block and chassis grounds carry the return current; a bad ground causes wrong sensing and dim lamps.
Higher temperature usually calls for a lower charge voltage, not higher.

quiz.q: State the purpose of the rectifier in the charging circuit.
quiz.a: It converts the alternator's three-phase AC into DC for the bus and battery.

quiz.q: Why does the charge warning lamp go out after the engine starts?
quiz.a: D+ rises to about bus voltage, so the voltage across the lamp falls to near zero and current through it stops.

quiz.q: An alternator is regulated at 14.4 V. The battery open-circuit voltage is 12.3 V and internal resistance is 0.015 Ω. Neglect wiring resistance. Find the initial charging current.
The charge warning lamp is open. The belt is tight and the battery is good. Will the alternator charge? Explain.
quiz.a: On a machine that uses the lamp for initial excitation, no. The field has no starting current, so the alternator may not build voltage. A dead bulb can stop charging.

quiz.q: What does the voltage sense wire do?
quiz.a: It carries the true bus voltage to the regulator with almost no current, so the regulator can set field current correctly.

quiz.q: At high electrical load, does the regulator increase or decrease field current? Why?
quiz.a: It increases field current. Bus voltage falls when load rises, so the regulator strengthens the field to raise alternator output and hold the set point.

quiz.q: After body repair, a car overcharges its battery. Which circuit connection is most suspect and why?
quiz.a: A ground or voltage-sense connection. If the regulator senses a low voltage because of a high-resistance ground or sense wire, it raises field current and overcharges.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production cars now use smart charging, where the ECU sets the alternator voltage based on battery temperature and state of charge, and turns charging off during acceleration to save fuel. Mild hybrids use a belt-driven starter-generator that recovers braking energy. Search terms: smart alternator, battery sensor, IBS, 48 V mild hybrid, and ISO 16750 for automotive electrical environments.
